docs.title: Home
docs.text: The H₂O–NaCl system at 250 bar, about the pressure at the seafloor at 2.5 km water depth. Shaded regions are where the fluid splits into two phases: vapour + liquid (pink), vapour + halite (grey) and liquid + halite (light blue). Elsewhere the fluid is a single phase, coloured by its density, which drops sharply between 380 and 400 °C. Seawater (dashed line) starts to separate into a vapour and a brine at about 388 °C. The phase-region geometry comes from Slice_constP, the densities from xthermo.tpx.

docs.title: xThermo
docs.text:
Phase relations and thermodynamic properties of H₂O–NaCl fluids from 0 to 1000 °C and 1 to 5000 bar, after Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007). A C++ library for simulation codes, with a Python interface for NumPy and Matplotlib.

Get started Gallery Model scope and limitations

docs.title: What xThermo computes
docs.text:
• Phase relations

    Liquid, vapour and halite, their two- and three-phase coexistence and the critical curve of the binary, as functions of temperature, pressure and salinity.

  • Fluid properties

    Density, specific enthalpy, heat capacity, viscosity and density derivatives of each phase and of the mixture, from T–p–X or H–p–X (enthalpy-based) input.

  • Python for science

    xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx evaluate whole NumPy grids, with an explicit error policy, and plotting helpers draw phase diagrams and property maps.

  • C++ for simulation codes

    A CMake package (find_package(xThermo)), exceptions or non-throwing evaluation with status codes, and one model instance per thread or MPI rank.

  • Pure water and NaCl

    Water from IAPS-84 (the basis of the Driesner model) or IAPWS-95; pure NaCl solid, liquid and vapour.

  • Checked against the literature

    Compared with the published tables of the Driesner papers and the IAPWS releases. Known differences and limitations are documented: Model scope and limitations.

docs.title: Seawater, heated at 250 bar
docs.text:
Following the dashed line of the figure above. Below about 388 °C seawater is a single liquid. Between 388 and 449 °C it splits into a vapour of low salinity and an increasingly saline brine; the vapour soon carries most of the mass. Above about 449 °C the brine is gone, and halite coexists with a vapour whose salinity keeps falling. This is the kind of phase separation seen in hydrothermal systems at mid-ocean ridges. Python code for both figures 
"""Homepage figures: the H2O-NaCl phase diagram at 250 bar with the density of the single-phase fluid, and seawater
heated at 250 bar.

Writes hero_desktop.png, hero_mobile.png and seawater_250bar.png to docs/assets/img (or the directory given as the
first argument or in $XTHERMO_FIGURE_DIR). Needs xthermo and matplotlib.
"""
import os

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st

st.apply()
OUT = st.outdir(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "assets", "img"))

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
P = 250e5                      # Pa
X_SEAWATER = 0.032             # kg/kg (3.2 wt% NaCl)

# fluid density on a T-X grid; the multiphase regions are drawn over it by plot_slice
T = np.linspace(1, 999, 400) + 273.15
X = np.logspace(-5, 0, 400)
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T[:, None], P, X[None, :], errors="nan")
section = sw.Slice_constP(P)

# seawater heated at 250 bar: where it separates into brine and vapour, and how salty each phase is
Tp = np.linspace(300, 600, 601) + 273.15
q = xthermo.tpx(sw, Tp, P, X_SEAWATER, errors="nan")
two_phase = q.has("vapour") & q.has("liquid")
vapour_mass = np.where(q.ok, q.S_v * q.Rho_v / q.Rho, np.nan)
tc = Tp - 273.15
T_SPLIT = tc[two_phase].min()       # °C, where seawater starts to separate into vapour and brine
T_HALITE = tc[two_phase].max()      # °C, above it vapour + halite


def phase_diagram(figsize, fontsize, labels, note, note_xy):
    with plt.rc_context({"font.size": fontsize}):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        field = xthermo.plot_property(ax, s, "Rho", x="X", y="T", cmap=st.OCEAN, vmin=0, vmax=1300, colorbar=False)
        xthermo.plot_slice(ax, section, x="X", y="T", points=False)
        ax.axvline(X_SEAWATER * 100, color=st.CORAL, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (5, 3)), zorder=5)
        ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 1000)
        ax.set_xlabel("bulk salinity (wt% NaCl)")
        ax.set_ylabel("temperature (°C)")
        cb = fig.colorbar(field["mesh"], ax=ax, pad=0.015, fraction=0.04, aspect=30)
        cb.set_label("density of the single-phase fluid (kg/m³)")
        cb.outline.set_visible(False)
        for x, y, text, colour in labels:
            ax.text(x, y, text, color=colour, ha="center", va="center", zorder=6)
        ax.text(X_SEAWATER * 100 * 1.12, 965, "seawater", color=st.CORAL, ha="left", va="top", zorder=6,
                fontweight="bold")
        ax.plot([X_SEAWATER * 100], [T_SPLIT], "o", ms=fontsize * 0.7, mfc=st.CORAL, mec="white", mew=1.5, zorder=7)
        ax.annotate(note, (X_SEAWATER * 100, T_SPLIT), xytext=note_xy, color="white", ha="right", va="center",
                    zorder=7, fontsize=fontsize * 0.9, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="white", lw=1))
        ax.set_title("H₂O–NaCl at 250 bar")
    return fig


desktop = phase_diagram((11, 5.2), 11, [
    (1.0, 870, "vapour + liquid", st.NAVY),
    (3, 600, "vapour + halite", st.INK),
    (68, 120, "liquid\n+ halite", st.NAVY),
    (5e-3, 110, "liquid-like fluid", "white"),
    (5e-3, 620, "vapour-like fluid", st.INK),
], f"seawater separates into\nvapour + brine at ≈{T_SPLIT:.0f} °C", (0.9, 250))
desktop.text(0.0, -0.02, st.CREDIT, fontsize=8, color=st.MUTED, transform=desktop.transFigure)
desktop.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "hero_desktop.png"))

mobile = phase_diagram((6.2, 6.4), 14, [
    (1.0, 870, "V + L", st.NAVY),
    (3, 600, "V + H", st.INK),
    (52, 110, "L+H", st.NAVY),
    (6e-3, 120, "liquid-like", "white"),
], f"splits at\n≈{T_SPLIT:.0f} °C", (0.9, 260))
mobile.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "hero_mobile.png"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
ax.axvspan(T_SPLIT, T_HALITE, color="#ddeef3", lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvspan(T_HALITE, tc[-1], color="#eeeeee", lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.semilogy(tc, np.where(q.has("liquid"), q.X_l * 100, np.nan), color=st.NAVY, lw=2.2, label="liquid (brine)")
ax.semilogy(tc, np.where(q.has("vapour"), q.X_v * 100, np.nan), color=st.CORAL, lw=2.2, label="vapour")
ax.set_ylabel("salinity of the phase (wt% NaCl)")
ax.set_xlabel("temperature (°C)")
ax.set_xlim(tc[0], tc[-1])
ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.86))
ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.spines["right"].set_visible(True)
ax2.plot(tc, vapour_mass * 100, color=st.TEAL, lw=1.4, ls="--")
ax2.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax2.set_ylabel("vapour mass fraction (%)", color=st.TEAL)
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", colors=st.TEAL)
ax.text((T_SPLIT + T_HALITE) / 2, 0.25, "vapour\n+ brine", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.text((T_HALITE + tc[-1]) / 2, 0.25, "vapour + halite", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.text((tc[0] + T_SPLIT) / 2, 0.25, "liquid", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.set_title("Seawater (3.2 wt% NaCl) heated at 250 bar")
fig.text(0.0, -0.03, st.CREDIT, fontsize=7.5, color=st.MUTED, transform=fig.transFigure)
fig.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "seawater_250bar.png"))
print("hero_desktop.png hero_mobile.png seawater_250bar.png written to", os.path.abspath(OUT))

The script uses a few shared style settings from docs/gallery/_style.py.

Authors
docs.text:
xThermo is developed at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel.

Zhikui Guo: original developer. He wrote the C++ library, the water and NaCl backends and the Python bindings, building on earlier GEOMAR MATLAB implementations of the Driesner model.

Lars Rüpke: scientific maintainer and project lead.

xThermo is used in hydrothermal-system modelling at GEOMAR, for example in the OpenFOAM-based solvers of HydrothermalFoam.

docs.title: How to cite
docs.text:
The equation of state implemented in xThermo is the work of Thomas Driesner and Christoph Heinrich. Please cite the two papers when you use xThermo:

Driesner, T. & Heinrich, C.A. (2007). The system H₂O–NaCl. Part I: Correlation formulae for phase relations in temperature–pressure–composition space from 0 to 1000 °C, 0 to 5000 bar, and 0 to 1 XNaCl. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 71, 4880–4901. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2007.05.026

Driesner, T. (2007). The system H₂O–NaCl. Part II: Correlations for molar volume, enthalpy, and isobaric heat capacity from 0 to 1000 °C, 1 to 5000 bar, and 0 to 1 XNaCl. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 71, 4902–4919. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2007.05.025

For the water properties, cite the formulation you use: IAPS-84 (Haar, Gallagher & Kell 1984, NBS/NRC Steam Tables, Hemisphere, Washington) or IAPWS-95 (Wagner & Pruß 2002, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 31, 387–535).

To refer to the software itself, cite it as xThermo, GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, https://github.com/lruepke/xThermo, with the version you used (xthermo.__version__). A citable DOI for xThermo is planned.

docs.title: Command-line tool
docs.text: After building and installing xThermo, the xThermal binary provides command-line access to the full EOS.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
xThermal [program] [arguments]
xThermal [program] -h          # help for a specific sub-program

Available sub-programs:

Program Description thermo Calculate thermodynamic properties from T-P-X or H-P-X input lutgen Generate an AMR lookup-table (binary .bin) lutinfo Print information about a lookup-table file lut2vtu Convert a lookup-table to VTU format for visualisation lookup Query an existing lookup-table at given T/H-P-X points

No spaces between flag and value

The argument parser requires the value to follow the flag letter immediately, with no space: -P300E5 ✓ — -P 300E5 ✗

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Quantity Flag Unit Temperature -T, -R °C Pressure -P, -R Pa Salinity -X, -R kg/kg (mass fraction 0–1; seawater = 0.032) Enthalpy -H, -R J/kg

In multiphase H₂O–NaCl states, the saturations in the output are volume fractions. The built-in help text calls them mass fractions, which applies only to pure water. Bulk viscosity and heat capacity of multiphase states are defined as described in Model scope and limitations.

docs.title: Required
docs.text:
Flag Description -D[0\|1\|2\|3] Calculation Dimension: 0 = scatter, 1 = 1-D, 2 = 2-D, 3 = 3-D -V… Independent Variables — must match -D (see table below) -Pval / -Tval / -Xval / -Hval Fixed value for variables not in -V -Rmin/step/max[/…] Range for each variable in -V order (1-D/2-D/3-D only)

Valid -V options by dimension:

-D Valid -V 0 PTX, PHX 1 T, P, X, H 2 PT, PX, TX, PH, HX 3 PTX, PHX

docs.title: Optional
docs.text: Flag Description -Gfile Input text file for scatter calculation (columns match -V order) -Ofile Output file — format from extension: .csv, .txt, .vtk -tN Number of OpenMP threads -n Normalise VTK output (2-D/3-D) -BIAPS84 Water backend: IAPS84 (default) or IAPWS95 -FH2O-NaCl Fluid: H2O-NaCl (default), H2O, NaCl

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The CLI and Python API give identical results. For T = 300 °C, P = 300 bar (300×10⁵ Pa), X = 0.1 kg/kg:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -P300E5 -T300 -X0.1

H2O-NaCl
T=300 deg.C = 573.15 K, P=300 bar, X=10 wt% NaCl, H=1.21693e+06 J/kg
  phase: Liquid
  Rho=849.034 [kg/m^3]
  H=1.21693e+06 [J/kg]
  Cp=4407.72 [J/kg/K]
  Mu=0.000114076 [Pa S]

Equivalent Python:

from xThermal import H2ONaCl
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
props = sw.UpdateState_TPX(300 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1)
print(props.Rho)   # 849.034 kg/m³

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
A few examples of what xThermo computes for hydrothermal fluids. Every figure is made by the Python script shown below it, with the published version of the library; the scripts run in the documentation's test suite. They use the phase-region colours of xthermo.plot_slice and a few shared style settings from docs/gallery/_style.py.

All results come from the H₂O–NaCl model of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007) with the IAPS-84 water backend. Where a figure touches a region in which the model's formulation is uncertain, the text says so; the Model scope and limitations page has the details.

More figures: the homepage (the phase diagram at 250 bar and seawater heated at 250 bar), and the phase diagrams and property maps of the Python guide.

docs.title: How the phase diagram changes with depth
docs.text:
The same temperature–salinity section at four pressures, roughly the pressures at the base of 1, 2.5, 4 and 10 km of seawater. At 100 bar a liquid of seawater salinity (dashed) starts to separate into vapour and brine at 312 °C. Between 341 and 771 °C it is vapour + halite: the brine has dried out and salt precipitates. With rising pressure the two-phase fields move to higher temperatures (separation of seawater at 388 °C at 250 bar, 447 °C at 400 bar and 688 °C at 1000 bar). The three-phase assemblage vapour + liquid + halite exists only up to 390 bar, so at 400 and 1000 bar halite and vapour no longer coexist. The halite liquidus on the salt-rich side (blue) barely moves.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
pressures = [100e5, 250e5, 400e5, 1000e5]        # Pa

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 4.4), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
handles = {}
for ax, p in zip(axes, pressures):
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    h = xthermo.plot_slice(ax, sw.Slice_constP(p), x="X", y="T", points=False)
    handles.update(h)
    ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)                       # wt% NaCl
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1000)                         # °C
    ax.set_title(f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar", loc="center")
    ax.axvline(3.2, color=st.CORAL, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 3)))   # seawater
    if ax is not axes[0]:
        ax.set_ylabel("")
# one legend entry for the three-phase assemblage (its temperature differs between the panels)
vlh = [k for k in handles if k.startswith("V+L+H")]
handles = {k: v for k, v in handles.items() if k not in vlh} | {"V+L+H (a line in T–X)": handles[vlh[0]]}
fig.legend(handles.values(), handles.keys(), loc="outside lower center", ncol=7, fontsize="small")
fig.suptitle("The H₂O–NaCl phase diagram at four pressures (dashed: seawater, 3.2 wt% NaCl)", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Rising seawater: boiling or condensation
docs.text:
Seawater heated at depth rises towards the seafloor and its pressure drops. This example follows three parcels that start at 500 bar and 380, 420 or 450 °C, keeping their specific enthalpy constant as the pressure falls: an idealised, adiabatic ascent with no heat exchanged with the surrounding rock and no change in kinetic or potential energy. Each path is computed with xthermo.hpx at the enthalpy of its starting state.

The two cooler fluids are liquid-like. They reach the two-phase field at 191 and 260 bar (dots) and boil: the vapour fraction grows from zero as the pressure falls, and the fluid cools along the boiling curve. The hottest fluid starts vapour-like (480 kg/m³), close to the critical curve of seawater-like compositions. It enters the two-phase field at 331 bar on the vapour side, so it does not boil: a small amount of brine condenses from it, and the vapour fraction starts near 100 %. At 50 bar all three are vapour + brine at about 266 °C. The library labels all three starting states "Liquid"; above the critical curve this label does not distinguish liquid-like from vapour-like fluids.

The small kinks where the paths cross 374 °C are where the model's vapour–liquid correlations change form at the critical temperature of water. Real upflow exchanges heat with the rock and mixes with other fluids, so these paths show the thermodynamics of decompression, not a model of a vent.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
X = 0.032                                        # seawater salinity, kg/kg
p = np.geomspace(500e5, 50e5, 300)               # decompression from 500 to 50 bar, Pa

# where seawater is a single phase or vapour + liquid, in temperature and pressure
T_grid = np.linspace(200, 500, 301) + 273.15
P_grid = np.geomspace(40e5, 550e5, 300)
grid = xthermo.tpx(sw, T_grid[None, :], P_grid[:, None], X, errors="nan")

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6), layout="constrained")
ax.set_yscale("log")
xthermo.plot_phases(ax, grid, x="T", y="P", legend=False)
ax.invert_yaxis()                                # pressure decreases upwards, as on the way to the seafloor

for T0, colour in [(380, st.NAVY), (420, st.TEAL), (450, st.CORAL)]:
    start = xthermo.tpx(sw, T0 + 273.15, p[0], X)            # the fluid at depth
    path = xthermo.hpx(sw, start.H, p, X, errors="nan")       # same specific enthalpy at every pressure
    ax.plot(path.T - 273.15, p / 1e5, color=colour, lw=2.2, label=f"starts at {T0} °C, 500 bar")
    boiling = path.has("vapour") & path.has("liquid")
    w_vapour = np.where(boiling, path.S_v * path.Rho_v / path.Rho, np.nan)   # vapour mass fraction (two phases only)
    bx.plot(p / 1e5, 100 * w_vapour, color=colour, lw=2.2)
    i = np.flatnonzero(boiling)[0]
    ax.plot(path.T[i] - 273.15, p[i] / 1e5, "o", ms=7, mfc=colour, mec="white", mew=1.5)

ticks = [50, 100, 200, 300, 500]                 # bar
ax.set_yticks(ticks, [str(t) for t in ticks])
ax.set_title("Path in temperature and pressure")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize="small")
ax.text(300, 300, "single-phase fluid", ha="center", fontsize="small")
ax.text(300, 75, "vapour + liquid", ha="center", fontsize="small")
ax.text(470, 70, "vapour\n+ halite", ha="center", fontsize="small")

bx.set_xscale("log")
bx.set_xticks(ticks, [str(t) for t in ticks])
bx.invert_xaxis()
bx.annotate("starts as a vapour-like fluid:\na brine condenses", (325, 70), xytext=(240, 88), fontsize="small",
            color=st.CORAL, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=st.CORAL))
bx.text(150, 8, "start as liquid-like fluids: they boil", fontsize="small", color=st.INK)
bx.set_xlabel("Pressure (bar)")
bx.set_ylabel("vapour mass fraction (%)")
bx.set_ylim(0, 100)
bx.set_title("Vapour mass fraction once two phases coexist")
fig.suptitle("Seawater rising from 500 bar at constant specific enthalpy (no heat exchange)", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Coexisting brine and vapour
docs.text:
Inside the vapour + liquid field a fluid splits into a dense, salty brine and a light, nearly salt-free vapour. The figure shows both phases along four isobars. The compositions are the library's V+L compositions (XL_VL, XV_VL), and the densities come from xthermo.tpx at a bulk salinity between the two, which lies inside the two-phase field.

At each pressure the two branches meet at the critical curve, where brine and vapour become identical. Away from it the density contrast, the driving force for the gravitational separation of the two phases, reaches 1000 kg/m³ and more, and the vapour carries orders of magnitude less salt than the brine. At 250 bar the two-phase field is interrupted between 449 and 716 °C, where vapour and halite coexist instead (see the first figure). Higher pressure brings the phases closer: the critical curve moves to higher temperature and the vapour holds more salt.

The figure stops at 800 °C. Above the melting point of NaCl (800.7 °C) the published equation for the vapour composition is incomplete, and xThermo's vapour salinities differ from those of the model author's program by up to about 24 % at 1000 °C (details). Brine densities above 600 °C below 390 bar use the model's high-temperature density extrapolation.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(380, 800, 421) + 273.15          # K; up to 800 °C (see the text)
colours = {250e5: st.CORAL, 400e5: st.TEAL, 600e5: "#1f6f9a", 1000e5: st.NAVY}

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6), layout="constrained")
for p, colour in colours.items():
    # compositions of the coexisting liquid and vapour; a bulk salinity between them lies in the two-phase field
    x_l = np.array(sw.XL_VL(T, np.full_like(T, p)))
    x_v = np.array(sw.XV_VL(T, np.full_like(T, p)))
    s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, p, 0.5 * (x_l + x_v), errors="nan", absent="nan")
    two_phase = s.ok & s.has("liquid") & s.has("vapour") & ~s.has("halite")
    rho_l = np.where(two_phase, s.Rho_l, np.nan)
    rho_v = np.where(two_phase, s.Rho_v, np.nan)
    label = f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar"
    ax.plot(T - 273.15, rho_l, color=colour, lw=2, label=label)
    ax.plot(T - 273.15, rho_v, color=colour, lw=2, ls="--")
    bx.semilogy(T - 273.15, np.where(two_phase, 100 * s.X_l, np.nan), color=colour, lw=2, label=label)
    bx.semilogy(T - 273.15, np.where(two_phase, 100 * s.X_v, np.nan), color=colour, lw=2, ls="--")

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("density (kg/m³)")
ax.set_title("Density: brine (solid) and vapour (dashed)")
ax.legend(fontsize="small")
bx.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
bx.set_ylabel("salinity (wt% NaCl)")
bx.set_title("Salinity: brine (solid) and vapour (dashed)")
bx.legend(fontsize="small", loc="lower right")
fig.suptitle("Coexisting brine and vapour in the vapour + liquid field of H₂O–NaCl", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Water near its critical point
docs.text:
Above its critical pressure (220.6 bar) water passes continuously from a dense, liquid-like state to a light, vapour-like one, without boiling. Where this change is fastest, the heat capacity has a sharp maximum: water then absorbs a lot of heat for a small temperature change. The maximum is highest and narrowest just above the critical pressure (230 bar) and broadens and shifts to higher temperatures with pressure. This matters for heat transport in hydrothermal systems at supercritical conditions.

The two water formulations available in xThermo (solid: IAPS-84, the basis of the H₂O–NaCl model; dotted: IAPWS-95) agree closely except near the maximum at 230 bar, where the peak heights differ by about 10 %. Close to the critical point both are less certain, and the published validity of IAPS-84 excludes a small region around it. The peak heights shown also depend on the 0.1 K temperature spacing.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2O

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
models = {"IAPS-84": H2O.cIAPS84(), "IAPWS-95": H2O.cIAPWS95()}
T = np.linspace(330, 480, 1501) + 273.15         # K, steps of 0.1 K
colours = {230e5: st.CORAL, 250e5: st.TEAL, 300e5: "#1f6f9a", 400e5: st.NAVY}

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4), layout="constrained")
for p, colour in colours.items():
    for (name, water), ls in zip(models.items(), ["-", ":"]):
        s = xthermo.tpx(water, T, p, errors="nan")
        label = f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar" if name == "IAPS-84" else None
        ax.semilogy(T - 273.15, s.Cp / 1e3, color=colour, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
        bx.plot(T - 273.15, s.Rho, color=colour, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("isobaric heat capacity (kJ/(kg K))")
ax.set_title("Heat capacity above the critical pressure")
ax.legend(title="solid: IAPS-84, dotted: IAPWS-95", fontsize="small", title_fontsize="small")
bx.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
bx.set_ylabel("density (kg/m³)")
bx.set_title("Density")
fig.suptitle("Pure water near its critical point (374 °C, 220.6 bar)", x=0.01, ha="left", color=st.NAVY,
             fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: The phase diagram in three dimensions
docs.text:
The sections above are slices through one three-dimensional structure in temperature, pressure and salinity. The vapour + liquid region is a dome bounded by its liquid limb (dark grey) and its vapour limb (light grey), which meet along the critical curve (red) on its crest. Below it lies the three-phase surface vapour + liquid + halite, which at each temperature has a single pressure and spans the salinities from the vapour to halite (blue and orange parts). Beneath that, vapour coexists with halite (purple: the vapour side). On the salt-rich side, the halite liquidus (green) separates liquid from liquid + halite.

The salinity axis is linear, so the vapour compositions, often below 0.01 wt% NaCl, lie close to the zero-salinity plane; the sections above show them on a logarithmic axis.

Python code 
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# ── VLH surface (V→L side and L→H side) ──────────────────────────────────
nT = 80
nT_high = nT // 3
T_high  = H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH + (sw.Tmax_VLH() - H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH) * 0.95
T_vlh   = np.append(np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, T_high, nT - nT_high),
                    np.linspace(T_high, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT_high))
P_vlh   = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vlh))
Xl_vlh, Xv_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T_vlh, P_vlh))

n_log, n_lin = 20, 40
nX = n_log + n_lin
TT_vlh = np.tile(T_vlh, (nX, 1))
PP_vlh = np.tile(P_vlh, (nX, 1))
XX_V2L = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
XX_L2H = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
for j in range(len(T_vlh)):
    XX_V2L[:, j] = np.append(
        10 ** np.linspace(np.log10(max(Xv_vlh[j], 1e-10)), np.log10(0.01), n_log),
        np.linspace(0.01, Xl_vlh[j], n_lin))
    XX_L2H[:, j] = np.linspace(Xl_vlh[j], 1.0, nX)

# ── VH surface ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
nP = 60
T_vh = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT)
P_vlh2 = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vh))
TT_vh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_vh = np.zeros_like(TT_vh)
np_low = nP // 3
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    p_low = sw.pmin() + (P_vlh2[i] - sw.pmin()) * 0.1
    PP_vh[:, i] = np.append(np.linspace(sw.pmin(), p_low, np_low),
                            np.linspace(p_low, P_vlh2[i], nP - np_low))
XX_VH = np.array(sw.X_VH(TT_vh.ravel(), PP_vh.ravel())).reshape(TT_vh.shape)

# ── Halite liquidus ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TT_lh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_lh = np.zeros_like(TT_lh)
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    PP_lh[:, i] = np.linspace(P_vlh2[i], 2500e5, nP)
XL_LH = np.array(sw.X_HaliteLiquidus(TT_lh.ravel(), PP_lh.ravel())).reshape(TT_lh.shape)

# ── VL surfaces ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pb_l = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Liquid)
pb_v = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Vapor)

# ── Critical curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T_crit = np.linspace(sw.get_pWater().T_critical(), sw.Tmax(), 80)
p_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T_crit))

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 9))
ax  = fig.add_subplot(111, projection='3d', facecolor='None')
legend = []   # 3-D surfaces give no usable legend handles: one coloured swatch per surface

def surf(TT, PP, XX, color, label):
    ax.plot_surface(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                    color=color, alpha=0.45, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                      color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.6, label=label))

surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_V2L,  'steelblue', 'VLH (V side)')
surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_L2H,  'orange',    'VLH (L+H side)')
surf(TT_vh,  PP_vh,  XX_VH,   'purple',    'VH surface')
surf(TT_lh,  PP_lh,  XL_LH,   'limegreen', 'Halite liquidus')

for pb, color, label in [(pb_l, 'black', 'VL liquid'), (pb_v, 'gray', 'VL vapor')]:
    T2 = np.array(pb.T); P2 = np.array(pb.p); X2 = np.array(pb.X)
    ax.plot_surface(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.4, label=label))

ax.plot(X_crit * 100, T_crit - 273.15, p_crit / 1e5, color='red', lw=2)
legend.append(Line2D([], [], color='red', lw=2, label='Critical curve'))
ax.plot(Xv_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='red',   lw=1)
ax.plot(Xl_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='green', lw=1)

ax.set_xlabel('Salinity (wt% NaCl)', fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel('Temperature (°C)',    fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_zlabel('Pressure (bar)',      fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 1000); ax.set_zlim(0, 2500)
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-145)
ax.set_title(r'H$_2$O–NaCl phase boundaries in T–p–X space', fontsize=13, pad=12)
ax.legend(handles=legend, loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.88)   # leaves room for the axis labels
plt.show()

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: xThermo is a C++ library with a Python interface. Python users build and install the package xthermo with pip; C++ users build and install the library with CMake. Both compile the library from source, which takes a few minutes.

docs.title: From source (current)
docs.text:
You need Python ≥ 3.10, a C/C++ compiler (gcc ≥ 11 or Apple clang) and make. pip takes CMake and SWIG from PyPI if they are not installed, and builds GSL from the official, checksum-verified release.

git clone https://github.com/lruepke/xThermo.git
cd xThermo
pip install .                 # or: pip install ".[plotting]" to add matplotlib

Use any environment you like (venv, conda, …). NumPy is installed as a dependency; Matplotlib is only needed for the plotting helpers.

Check the installation:

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)      # T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]
print(xthermo.__version__, s.phase_name, s.Rho)

The former package name still works: from xThermal import H2ONaCl gives the same modules.

docs.text:

pip install xthermo

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependency Required Notes C++ compiler (gcc ≥ 11 or Apple clang) yes the code is compiled as C++11 CMake ≥ 3.18 yes GSL 2.x yes from the system, or built from source by CMake (see below) SWIG ≥ 4 and Python ≥ 3.10 with headers for the Python modules skip with -DXTHERMO_PYTHON=OFF PROST 4.1 bundled the IAPS-84 water backend; compiled automatically

GSL from your package manager:

brew install gsl              # macOS
sudo apt install libgsl-dev   # Debian/Ubuntu
conda install -c conda-forge gsl

For a GSL in a non-standard location add -DGSL_ROOT_DIR=<prefix>. Without a system GSL, add -DXTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL=ON: CMake then downloads the official GSL 2.8 release from ftp.gnu.org, checks its SHA-256 checksum and builds it. For offline builds, point -DXTHERMO_GSL_ARCHIVE=<path to gsl-2.8.tar.gz> to a local copy of the same archive.

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install
cmake --build build -j
cmake --install build

The build type is Release unless -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is given. Options:

Option Default Description XTHERMO_PYTHON ON Build the Python modules (SWIG) XTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL OFF Build the pinned GSL release from source instead of using the system GSL XTHERMO_OPENMP OFF Use OpenMP for batch and lookup-table evaluation BUILD_SHARED_LIBS OFF Build the C++ library as a shared library XTHERMO_BUILD_TESTS OFF Build the developer test programs (ctest)

cmake --install creates:

install/
├── bin/xThermal                 # command-line tool
├── include/xThermo/             # C++ headers
├── lib/libxThermal.a            # C++ library
├── lib/cmake/xThermo/           # CMake package: find_package(xThermo)
└── API/python/cp3.13/           # Python modules; the name follows the Python version used by CMake
    ├── xthermo/                 # __init__.py, H2O.py, NaCl.py, H2ONaCl.py, _H2O.so, _NaCl.so, _H2ONaCl.so, ...

docs.title: Model scope and limitations
docs.text: xThermo implements the H₂O–NaCl correlations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), combined with an equation of state for pure water. This page states what the implementation computes, where it differs from other implementations of the same model, and how it behaves outside the model domain.

docs.title: Model domain and runtime checks
docs.text:
The correlations are published for 0–1000 °C, 1–5000 bar and X_NaCl = 0–1. The H₂O–NaCl class reports this domain as Tmin() = 273.16 K, Tmax() = 1273.15 K, pmin() = 1e5 Pa and pmax() = 5e8 Pa.

Only part of the domain is enforced at run time:

Input Behaviour T > 1273.15 K error (UpdateState_TPX, findPhaseRegion_TPX) H above the enthalpy at 1273.15 K error (UpdateState_HPX) p < 1 bar not checked: values are returned p > 5000 bar "IAPS84": not checked, values are returned; "IAPWS95": error from the water backend X > 1 not checked: values are returned (e.g. X = 1.2 gives an "L+H" state) X < 0 error from the water backend

Results outside the published domain are extrapolations of the correlations and have not been validated. Check your inputs before calling the library.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• C++: errors are thrown as exceptions derived from xThermal::xThermalBaseError (Exception.h), for example OutOfRangeError, ValueError and NotImplementedError.
  • Python: these appear as built-in exceptions:
C++ error Python exception out of range, invalid value ValueError not implemented (e.g. an unknown backend name) NotImplementedError solver failure, other errors RuntimeError
  • Array calls: a call with NumPy arrays stops at the first point that fails and returns no partial result. To keep the valid points, evaluate point by point and catch the exception.
  • Helper functions: some phase-boundary helpers do not raise outside their own temperature range. They print a warning and return 0 (for example X_Critical for T outside the critical-curve range).

docs.title: Water backends
docs.text:
Backend Formulation Range of the pure-water class "IAPS84" (default of the command-line tool) IAPS-84 (Haar, Gallagher & Kell 1984), computed with PROST 4.1 260–2500 K, up to 30 000 bar "IAPWS95" IAPWS-95 (Wagner & Pruß 2002) 273.165–2273.15 K, up to 5000 bar

Notes: - The Driesner correlations were fitted with IAPS-84. "IAPS84" is therefore the reference backend. - Most phase-boundary correlations do not depend on the backend: for example the V+L+H pressure, and the critical curve and V+L compositions above 500 °C. - Below 500 °C, the critical pressure with "IAPWS95" is up to about 0.07 % higher than with "IAPS84". Its critical curve has a step of about 0.03 % at 500 °C. - Below 500 °C, V+L vapour compositions differ between the backends by up to about 2.5 %. - Densities, enthalpies and heat capacities of the brine differ slightly between the backends, because they are evaluated through the water equation of state. - Any other backend name raises NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Phase properties and bulk properties
docs.text:
Each phase has its own properties: Rho_l, H_l, Cp_l, Mu_l, X_l for the liquid; _v for the vapour; _h for halite. They are computed from the published correlations.

The bulk fields are defined as follows:

Field Single phase Two or three phases S_l, S_v, S_h 1 for the present phase volume fractions of the phases (H₂O–NaCl). The pure-water classes in xThermal.H2O report mass fractions instead. Rho phase density Σ S_i ρ_i H phase enthalpy mass-weighted: Σ S_i ρ_i h_i / ρ Cp (∂h/∂T)_{P,X} of the phase (Driesner 2007, Eq. 27) mass-weighted phase heat capacities, Σ S_i ρ_i c_P,i / ρ, at fixed phase amounts and compositions. Contains no latent heat and is not the derivative of the bulk enthalpy. Example: in V+L at 400 °C, 250 bar, 10 wt % it is 9.2 kJ/(kg K), whereas (∂H/∂T)_{P,X} of the bulk is 31 kJ/(kg K). In V+L+H, Cp is 0. Mu phase viscosity not defined. Mu is a placeholder value of 1 in V+L, L+H and V+H. Only two H–P–X branches set S_l μ_l + S_v μ_v: V+L+H, and the low-salinity / low-pressure V+L fallback. The same V+L state can therefore report 1 or a weighted value, depending on the call. Use Mu_l and Mu_v. dRhodT, dRhodP, IsobaricExpansivity, IsothermalCompressibility phase derivatives not defined as bulk quantities (the first three are 0); use the phase fields *_l, *_v

How bulk heat capacity and bulk viscosity of multiphase states should be defined is an open question. The fields above may change when it is decided.

docs.title: Differences from other implementations of the model
docs.text:
Other implementations of the same model include the author's SoWat program, his tabulated supplementary data, ProBrine and earlier GEOMAR MATLAB code. Three differences between them and xThermo are known and deliberate.

Heat capacity. - xThermo: c_P = (∂h/∂T)_{P,X}, the published Eq. 27. It is consistent with the enthalpy. - SoWat 0.2 and ProBrine multiply Eq. 27 by 1/(1 + x), where x is the NaCl mole fraction of the phase. They do not change the enthalpy. - This factor is not part of the published formulation, and its justification has not been documented. Applied to c_P alone, it makes c_P inconsistent with the enthalpy, so xThermo does not apply it. - Consequence: SoWat and ProBrine heat capacities of saline phases are lower by 1/(1 + x). That is about 1 % for seawater, 9 % at 26 wt % and up to 50 % for nearly pure NaCl liquid.

Liquid enthalpy above 600 °C and below about 390 bar. - This applies to the liquid phase at T ≥ 600 °C and p ≤ 390.15 bar. There, the published enthalpy correlation can map the brine onto a water state in the vapour field, where it is not usable. - xThermo uses a smooth extrapolation adopted from earlier GEOMAR code. It has the same form as the published density extrapolation, and its heat capacity is consistent with it. - It differs from the author's tabulated values by up to about 3 %, which corresponds to −19 to +28 K in the temperature of a given enthalpy. - This is a difference between two implementations. The physical accuracy in this region has not been established.

Vapour composition in V+L above 800.7 °C. - Above the triple point of NaCl, the published vapour-composition equation (Driesner & Heinrich 2007, Eq. 15) contains a term that is not defined. - xThermo sets it to 1. This is consistent with the published condition that the NaCl boiling curve bounds the V+L field from below. - The author's program uses an undocumented temperature-dependent value instead. Against it, xThermo's vapour NaCl content is about 1.3 % lower at 810 °C and up to about 24 % lower at 1000 °C. - Below 800.7 °C, xThermo reproduces the author's tabulated compositions. - Available experimental data do not decide between the two treatments.

docs.title: Linking with CMake (recommended)
docs.text:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.18)
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(xThermo REQUIRED)

add_executable(my_app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE xThermo::xThermal)

Tell CMake where xThermo is installed:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/path/to/xThermo/install    # or: export xThermo_DIR=/path/to/xThermo/install
cmake --build build

The target xThermo::xThermal brings its include directory and its GSL dependency with it.

docs.title: Linking with g++ directly
docs.text:
export xThermo_DIR=/path/to/xThermo/install

g++ -std=c++11 \
    -I${xThermo_DIR}/include/xThermo $(gsl-config --cflags) \
    -o my_app main.cpp \
    -L${xThermo_DIR}/lib -lxThermal $(gsl-config --libs)

GSL

xThermo uses GSL for root finding (saturation pressure, phase boundaries, the H–p–X flash), so programs link GSL as well. gsl-config comes with the system GSL. If xThermo was built with -DXTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL=ON, GSL is installed with it: use -I${xThermo_DIR}/lib/xThermo/gsl/include and -L${xThermo_DIR}/lib/xThermo/gsl/lib -lgsl -lgslcblas instead of gsl-config.

All C++ functions use SI units unless noted otherwise in the source comments:

Quantity Unit Temperature K Pressure Pa Composition X kg/kg (mass fraction) Density kg/m³ Enthalpy J/kg

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Errors are thrown as exceptions derived from xThermal::xThermalBaseError (Exception.h), for example OutOfRangeError for T above 1273.15 K. See Model scope and limitations.

docs.title: VLH coexistence pressure
docs.text:
P_VLH returns the pressure on the three-phase V+L+H surface for a given temperature.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    int N = 100;
    double T_min = H2ONaCl::T_MIN_VLH;
    double T_max = H2ONaCl::T_MAX_VLH;
    double dT = (T_max - T_min) / (N - 1);

    std::cout << "T(°C)    P_VLH(bar)\n";
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        double T = T_min + i * dT;   // K
        double P = eos.P_VLH(T);     // Pa
        std::cout << T - 273.15 << "    " << P / 1e5 << "\n";
    }
}

docs.title: Phase region
docs.text:
findPhaseRegion_TPX returns the phase region index without computing all thermodynamic properties.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    double T = 400 + 273.15;   // K
    double p = 200e5;           // Pa  (200 bar)
    double X = 0.032;           // kg/kg  (3.2 wt% NaCl)

    PhaseRegion region = eos.findPhaseRegion_TPX(T, p, X);
    std::string name = eos.phase_name(region);

    std::cout << "Phase region: " << name << " (index " << region << ")\n";
}

docs.title: Phase region names
docs.text:
Names returned by phase_name for H₂O–NaCl states:

Name Enum value Description Liquid SinglePhase_L Single liquid phase. Single-phase "liquid-like" and "vapour-like" fluid above the critical curve are also reported as Liquid. Vapor SinglePhase_V Single vapour phase V+L TwoPhase_VL Vapour–liquid coexistence L+H TwoPhase_LH Liquid–halite coexistence V+H TwoPhase_VH Vapour–halite coexistence V+L+H ThreePhase_VLH Three-phase coexistence (reached through the H–p–X flash)

For pure water, the names of the water backend are used instead, for example Supercritical and Sup.crit. liquid, and V+L(water) in the two-phase region. This applies to the pure-water classes and also to cH2ONaCl at X = 0, which evaluates pure water directly.

docs.title: T-p-X calculation
docs.text:
UpdateState_TPX computes all thermodynamic properties for a given temperature, pressure, and salinity.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");   // backend: "IAPS84" or "IAPWS95"

    double T = 300 + 273.15;   // K
    double p = 300e5;           // Pa  (300 bar)
    double X = 0.1;             // kg/kg  (10 wt% NaCl)

    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    eos.UpdateState_TPX(props, T, p, X);

    std::cout << "Phase:    " << eos.phase_name(props.phase) << "\n"
              << "Density:  " << props.Rho                   << " kg/m³\n"
              << "Enthalpy: " << props.H / 1e6               << " MJ/kg\n"
              << "Cp:       " << props.Cp                    << " J/kg/K\n"
              << "Viscosity: " << props.Mu                   << " Pa·s\n";
}

docs.title: Python guide
docs.text:
The Python package xthermo gives you the H₂O–NaCl equation of state of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), pure water (IAPS-84, IAPWS-95) and pure NaCl. You evaluate states on NumPy arrays of any shape and draw phase diagrams and property maps with a few Matplotlib helpers.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")                         # H2O-NaCl with the IAPS-84 water backend

T = np.array([300.0, 400.0, 500.0]) + 273.15            # K
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)                    # p = 250 bar in Pa, X = 3.2 wt% NaCl in kg/kg
print(s.phase_name)                                     # ['Liquid' 'V+L' 'V+H']
print(s.Rho)                                            # bulk density, kg/m³
print(s.X_v)                                            # salinity of the vapour phase, kg/kg (0 where absent)

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
Module Class System xthermo.H2ONaCl cH2ONaCl("IAPS84"), cH2ONaCl("IAPWS95") H₂O–NaCl; the argument selects the water equation of state xthermo.H2O cIAPS84(), cIAPWS95() pure water xthermo.NaCl cNaCl("IAPS84") pure NaCl (solid, liquid, vapour)

The Driesner correlations were fitted with IAPS-84, so "IAPS84" is the reference backend for H₂O–NaCl. "IAPWS95" gives slightly different brine properties; see Model scope and limitations.

Create a model once and reuse it for all your evaluations. A model object is not meant to be shared between threads; use one per thread.

Inputs and outputs are in SI units everywhere:

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: pip install . in a clone of the repository installs xthermo with NumPy; pip install ".[plotting]" adds Matplotlib. See Installation. import xthermo loads only the compiled modules; NumPy and Matplotlib are imported when you first use tpx / hpx or a plotting helper.

docs.title: Classic SWIG interface
docs.text: The model classes also expose the library's C++ methods directly, through SWIG. xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx are built on them and are usually more convenient. The classic methods remain useful for single points in a loop (they avoid the small overhead of creating a States object) and for existing scripts.

docs.title: Single points
docs.text:
UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X) and UpdateState_HPX(H, p, X) return one ThermodynamicProperties object. Its fields are the same as those of States (see the field table), as plain Python numbers. The water and NaCl models take UpdateState_TPX(T, p).

from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

props = sw.UpdateState_TPX(300 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1)       # 300 °C, 300 bar, 10 wt% NaCl
print(sw.phase_name(props.phase), f"{props.Rho:.1f} kg/m³", f"{props.H/1e6:.4f} MJ/kg")

props = sw.UpdateState_HPX(1.5e6, 300e5, 0.05)            # H in J/kg
print(f"{props.T - 273.15:.1f} °C", sw.phase_name(props.phase))

Errors raise Python exceptions: ValueError for invalid or out-of-range input, RuntimeError for a failed solution, NotImplementedError for an unknown backend name. These are the base classes of the more specific exceptions that tpx and hpx raise (Errors and status).

docs.title: 1-D vectors
docs.text:
The same methods take three 1-D lists or arrays of equal length and return an object whose fields are SWIG vectors; convert them with np.array(...). There is no broadcasting: pass every input at full length. If any point fails, the whole call raises and returns nothing.

import numpy as np
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

T = np.linspace(100 + 273.15, 600 + 273.15, 200)
p = np.full_like(T, 300e5)
X = np.full_like(T, 0.1)

state = sw.UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X)
rho = np.array(state.Rho)
phase = np.array(state.phase)

The equivalent with the NumPy interface is xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 300e5, 0.1), which broadcasts the scalars, returns NumPy arrays and offers errors="nan". Its values are identical to the classic calls.

The vector form of UpdateState_TPX is not available on the pure-water classes in Python; use xthermo.tpx there.

docs.title: Other methods
docs.text:
Every model object also has, among others:

Method Returns phase_name(code) the name of a phase-region code Tmin(), Tmax(), pmin(), pmax() the range the model declares (K, Pa); see Model scope and limitations for what is checked T_critical(), p_critical() the critical point of water (water models) name() the model's name

The H₂O–NaCl model adds the phase-boundary functions (Phase boundaries) and the sections Slice_constP / Slice_constT (Phase diagrams).

docs.title: The former name xThermal
docs.text:
The package used to be imported as xThermal. That name still works and gives the same modules:

import xthermo
from xThermal import H2ONaCl          # the same module as xthermo.H2ONaCl

print(H2ONaCl is xthermo.H2ONaCl)    # True

New code should use import xthermo.

docs.title: Errors and status
docs.text: A point cannot always be evaluated: the input can be invalid (a NaN, a negative pressure), outside the range of the model (above 1000 °C for H₂O–NaCl), or a numerical solution can fail. tpx and hpx handle this with the errors argument.

docs.title: errors="raise" (the default)
docs.text:
errors="raise" is the default. If any point cannot be evaluated, the call raises an exception for the first such point (in C order). Its message names the point's index and inputs, the library's message and how many further points failed:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.array([300.0, 5000.0, np.nan])                 # K: valid, above the model range, invalid
try:
    xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)
except xthermo.EvaluationError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)                           # OutOfRangeError
    print(e.index, e.status, e.inputs)                # (1,) Status.OutOfRange {'T': 5000.0, 'p': 25000000.0, 'X': 0.032}
    print(e)                                          # the full message, ending in "[1 further failure]"

The exception classes are subclasses of xthermo.EvaluationError and of the matching built-in exception, so existing except ValueError code keeps working:

Exception Also a Status Cause xthermo.InvalidInputError ValueError InvalidInput non-finite T, H or p; p ≤ 0; X < 0 or non-finite X (H₂O–NaCl) xthermo.OutOfRangeError ValueError OutOfRange outside the range in which the model evaluates, e.g. T > 1273.15 K for H₂O–NaCl xthermo.NotConvergedError RuntimeError NotConverged a numerical solution failed, e.g. IAPWS-95 water exactly at its saturation pressure xthermo.NotAvailableError ValueError NotAvailable not implemented for this model or state, e.g. hpx with the pure NaCl model xthermo.EvaluationError Exception Failed any other error reported by the library

Each exception has the attributes index (a tuple; () for scalar input), status, inputs (a dict) and message (the library's message).

docs.title: errors="nan"
docs.text:
With errors="nan" the call never raises for points that cannot be evaluated. Those points are NaN in every number field (their inputs are kept), their phase is Unknown, and their status says why:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.array([300.0, 5000.0, np.nan])
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032, errors="nan")

print(s.ok)                                           # [ True False False]
print([xthermo.Status(int(c)).name for c in s.status])   # ['Ok', 'OutOfRange', 'InvalidInput']
print(s.Rho)                                          # [value, nan, nan]
for index, status, message in s.failures:
    print(index, status.name, message[:60])

This is the policy for grids and maps: evaluate everything, then use s.ok to select or mask. The plotting helpers draw points that were not evaluated in grey.

Errors that are not about a point, such as running out of memory or a programming error, are raised in both modes.

docs.title: Status values
docs.text:
xthermo.Status is an integer enumeration; s.status holds these integers (a single Status for scalar input).

Status Value Meaning Ok 0 evaluated InvalidInput 1 invalid input (non-finite, p ≤ 0, X < 0) OutOfRange 2 outside the range in which the model evaluates NotConverged 3 a numerical solution failed NotAvailable 4 not implemented or not available for this model or state Failed 5 any other error of the library

docs.title: Failed points and absent phases
docs.text:
A point that was not evaluated and a phase that is not present at an evaluated point are different things:

Question Test Was the point evaluated? s.ok Is there vapour at an evaluated point? s.has("vapour") (False at failed points) Evaluated, but without vapour? s.ok & ~s.has("vapour")

By default the fields of an absent phase are 0, as in the library; with absent="nan" they are NaN (see Evaluating states). Failed points are NaN in both cases.

docs.title: What is checked, and what is not
docs.text: The library rejects non-finite inputs, non-positive pressure and negative salinity, and H₂O–NaCl temperatures above 1273.15 K. It does not reject every input outside the published model domain (0–1000 °C, 1–5000 bar, X = 0–1): pressures below 1 bar are evaluated as extrapolations, and a salinity above 1, which is not physical, is evaluated too. Check your inputs against the domain; see Model scope and limitations.

docs.title: Evaluating states
docs.text:
Two functions evaluate the equation of state on scalars or NumPy arrays:

xthermo.tpx(model, T, p, X=0.0, *, errors="raise", absent="zero")   # temperature, pressure, salinity
xthermo.hpx(model, H, p, X=0.0, *, errors="raise", absent="zero")   # specific enthalpy, pressure, salinity
  • model is any model object: H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl(...), H2O.cIAPS84(), H2O.cIAPWS95() or NaCl.cNaCl(...).
  • T in K, p in Pa, H in J/kg, X in kg/kg. The water models ignore X.
  • The result is a xthermo.States object (below). hpx also returns the temperature, in T.
  • errors and absent choose how failed points and absent phases are reported: see Errors and status and Absent phases below.

docs.title: Scalars, arrays and broadcasting
docs.text:
The inputs can be numbers, lists or NumPy arrays of any shape that broadcast together. Every result array has the broadcast shape. A typical grid puts one input along each axis:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(100, 600, 6) + 273.15           # 6 temperatures, K
X = np.array([0.001, 0.032, 0.1, 0.3])          # 4 salinities, kg/kg

s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T[:, None], 300e5, X[None, :])
print(s.shape)                                  # (6, 4): temperature along axis 0, salinity along axis 1
print(s.Rho.round(1))                           # bulk density, kg/m³
print(s.phase_name[:, 1])                       # phases of 3.2 wt% NaCl from 100 to 600 °C

With scalar inputs every field is a single NumPy number:

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)          # 300 °C, 300 bar, 10 wt% NaCl
print(s.phase_name, round(float(s.Rho), 1), "kg/m³", round(float(s.H) / 1e6, 4), "MJ/kg")

All points are evaluated in one call into the C++ library. With the IAPS-84 backend a brine state takes a few microseconds; IAPWS-95 brines are slower (tenths of a millisecond), because the water equation of state is solved iteratively.

docs.title: The States result
docs.text:
Fields are read with attribute or key access, s.Rho or s["Rho"]; s.keys() lists them. Each field is a read-only NumPy array; use s.Rho.copy() for a writable one. Arrays stay valid after the model is deleted.

Attribute Content shape shape of the broadcast inputs fluid name of the model's fluid, e.g. "H2O-NaCl" phase phase-region code of each point (integer, table below) phase_name the name of each code, e.g. "V+L" (array of strings, or a string for scalar input) has(phase) mask: "liquid", "vapour" (or "vapor") or "halite" is present at an evaluated point status xthermo.Status of each point; Status.Ok for evaluated points (Errors and status) ok mask of the evaluated points (status == Status.Ok) failures list of (index, Status, message) for the points that were not evaluated

docs.title: Phase identification
docs.text:
phase holds the library's phase-region code. Its name is s.phase_name, or model.phase_name(code).

Code Name Phases present (has) 0 Liquid liquid 1 Vapor vapour 2 Solid halite (pure NaCl) 3, 4, 5 Supercritical, Sup.crit. vapor, Sup.crit. liquid one fluid phase, reported in the liquid fields (_l) 6 Critical point as 3 7 V+L(water) liquid, vapour (pure water at its boiling curve) 8 L+H liquid, halite 9 V+H vapour, halite 10 V+L liquid, vapour 11 V+L+H liquid, vapour, halite 12 Unknown none: the point was not evaluated

The labels "Liquid" and "Vapor" for a single-phase H₂O–NaCl fluid follow the library's classification. Above the critical curve of the mixture the fluid changes continuously between the two; there is no phase boundary there.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(300, 600, 7) + 273.15
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)             # seawater salinity, heated at 250 bar

two_phase = s.has("vapour") & s.has("liquid")    # where seawater has split into vapour and brine
print(T[two_phase] - 273.15)
print(s.X_l[two_phase], s.X_v[two_phase])        # brine and vapour salinity, kg/kg

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Each property comes as a bulk value and, where it applies, as phase values with the suffixes _l (liquid), _v (vapour) and _h (halite). In a single-phase state the bulk value is the value of that phase. In multiphase states the bulk fields have specific meanings, listed in the last column.

Field Unit Meaning In multiphase states (V+L, V+H, L+H, V+L+H) T, p, X K, Pa, kg/kg temperature, pressure, bulk salinity the inputs (T evaluated by hpx) H J/kg specific enthalpy mass-weighted: Σ Si ρi hi / ρ Rho kg/m³ density Σ Si ρi Cp J/(kg K) isobaric heat capacity (∂h/∂T)p,X "frozen" mass-weighted phase heat capacity Σ Si ρi cp,i / ρ, which contains no latent heat and is not ∂H/∂T of the mixture; 0 in V+L+H Mu Pa s dynamic viscosity not a mixture viscosity: 1 in V+L, V+H and L+H; use Mu_l, Mu_v and the saturations S_l, S_v, S_h – phase saturations volume fractions of liquid, vapour and halite (H₂O–NaCl). The water models report the vapour mass fraction (quality) in their two-phase states X_l, X_v kg/kg salinity of the liquid and the vapour phase compositions of the coexisting phases Rho_l, Rho_v, Rho_h kg/m³ phase densities H_l, H_v, H_h J/kg phase specific enthalpies Cp_l, Cp_v, Cp_h J/(kg K) phase heat capacities at fixed phase composition Mu_l, Mu_v Pa s phase viscosities; NaN where the viscosity correlation does not evaluate dRhodT, dRhodT_l, dRhodT_v kg/(m³ K) ∂ρ/∂T at fixed p (and composition) bulk value not computed (0) dRhodP, dRhodP_l, dRhodP_v kg/(m³ Pa) ∂ρ/∂p at fixed T (and composition) bulk value not computed (0) IsothermalCompressibility, IsothermalCompressibility_l, IsothermalCompressibility_v 1/Pa (1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂p at fixed T bulk: the equilibrium derivative at fixed T and bulk X (the phases re-equilibrate); 0 in V+L+H IsobaricExpansivity, IsobaricExpansivity_l, IsobaricExpansivity_v 1/K −(1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂T at fixed p bulk value not computed (0)

Convert saturations to mass fractions with wi = Si ρi / ρ. The pure NaCl model reports its properties in the bulk fields only. More on these conventions and on the model's validity: Model scope and limitations.

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 400 + 273.15, 250e5, 0.1)    # 400 °C, 250 bar, 10 wt% NaCl: vapour + liquid

w_v = s.S_v * s.Rho_v / s.Rho                     # vapour mass fraction from the volume fraction
print(s.phase_name, f"vapour: {float(s.S_v):.3f} of the volume, {float(w_v):.3f} of the mass")
print(f"liquid {float(s.X_l):.4f} kg/kg, {float(s.Rho_l):.1f} kg/m³; vapour {float(s.X_v):.2e} kg/kg, {float(s.Rho_v):.1f} kg/m³")

docs.title: Absent phases
docs.text:
In the library's results the fields of a phase that is not present hold 0: Rho_v of a pure liquid, for example. That is the default, absent="zero". With absent="nan" these phase fields are NaN instead, which keeps absent phases out of plots and statistics:

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.array([300.0, 400.0, 500.0]) + 273.15
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032, absent="nan")
print(s.phase_name)                               # Liquid, V+L, V+H
print(s.Rho_v)                                    # NaN where there is no vapour
print(s.Rho_l)                                    # NaN where there is no liquid
print(s.S_v)                                      # saturations are never changed: 0 where absent

absent="nan" affects only the phase fields (_l, _v, _h, except the saturations) of the States result. Bulk fields and the library's own results are unchanged. Whether a phase is present follows the phase code; has() gives the same mask.

docs.title: Enthalpy-based input
docs.text:
hpx inverts the enthalpy: it finds the state with the given specific enthalpy, pressure and salinity, and returns it with its temperature.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
H = np.array([1.0e6, 2.0e6, 3.0e6])               # J/kg
s = xthermo.hpx(sw, H, 300e5, 0.05)               # 300 bar, 5 wt% NaCl
print(s.T - 273.15)                               # °C
print(s.phase_name)

The field H of the result is the enthalpy of the returned state. It agrees with the input to within the solver tolerance. For plots on an enthalpy grid, use the input values as coordinates (see Property maps). The pure NaCl model has no enthalpy-based input (hpx raises NotAvailableError).

docs.title: Phase boundaries
docs.text:
The model object cH2ONaCl computes the phase boundaries of the H₂O–NaCl system directly: the three-phase surface V+L+H, the critical curve, the halite liquidus and the compositions of coexisting phases. For complete sections through the phase diagram use Phase diagrams; for properties on grids, Evaluating states. The Gallery shows how the phase diagram changes with pressure.

These functions take and return SI units (K, Pa, kg/kg). They accept NumPy arrays, but return tuples or lists: wrap the results in np.array(...), as in the examples below.

docs.title: 3-D overview
docs.text:
The full phase boundary structure in T–p–X space, showing the VLH surface, VH surface, halite liquidus, VL two-phase surfaces, and the critical curve.

Code to reproduce this figure 
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# ── VLH surface (V→L side and L→H side) ──────────────────────────────────
nT = 80
nT_high = nT // 3
T_high  = H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH + (sw.Tmax_VLH() - H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH) * 0.95
T_vlh   = np.append(np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, T_high, nT - nT_high),
                    np.linspace(T_high, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT_high))
P_vlh   = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vlh))
Xl_vlh, Xv_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T_vlh, P_vlh))

n_log, n_lin = 20, 40
nX = n_log + n_lin
TT_vlh = np.tile(T_vlh, (nX, 1))
PP_vlh = np.tile(P_vlh, (nX, 1))
XX_V2L = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
XX_L2H = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
for j in range(len(T_vlh)):
    XX_V2L[:, j] = np.append(
        10 ** np.linspace(np.log10(max(Xv_vlh[j], 1e-10)), np.log10(0.01), n_log),
        np.linspace(0.01, Xl_vlh[j], n_lin))
    XX_L2H[:, j] = np.linspace(Xl_vlh[j], 1.0, nX)

# ── VH surface ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
nP = 60
T_vh = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT)
P_vlh2 = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vh))
TT_vh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_vh = np.zeros_like(TT_vh)
np_low = nP // 3
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    p_low = sw.pmin() + (P_vlh2[i] - sw.pmin()) * 0.1
    PP_vh[:, i] = np.append(np.linspace(sw.pmin(), p_low, np_low),
                            np.linspace(p_low, P_vlh2[i], nP - np_low))
XX_VH = np.array(sw.X_VH(TT_vh.ravel(), PP_vh.ravel())).reshape(TT_vh.shape)

# ── Halite liquidus ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TT_lh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_lh = np.zeros_like(TT_lh)
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    PP_lh[:, i] = np.linspace(P_vlh2[i], 2500e5, nP)
XL_LH = np.array(sw.X_HaliteLiquidus(TT_lh.ravel(), PP_lh.ravel())).reshape(TT_lh.shape)

# ── VL surfaces ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pb_l = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Liquid)
pb_v = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Vapor)

# ── Critical curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T_crit = np.linspace(sw.get_pWater().T_critical(), sw.Tmax(), 80)
p_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T_crit))

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 9))
ax  = fig.add_subplot(111, projection='3d', facecolor='None')
legend = []   # 3-D surfaces give no usable legend handles: one coloured swatch per surface

def surf(TT, PP, XX, color, label):
    ax.plot_surface(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                    color=color, alpha=0.45, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                      color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.6, label=label))

surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_V2L,  'steelblue', 'VLH (V side)')
surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_L2H,  'orange',    'VLH (L+H side)')
surf(TT_vh,  PP_vh,  XX_VH,   'purple',    'VH surface')
surf(TT_lh,  PP_lh,  XL_LH,   'limegreen', 'Halite liquidus')

for pb, color, label in [(pb_l, 'black', 'VL liquid'), (pb_v, 'gray', 'VL vapor')]:
    T2 = np.array(pb.T); P2 = np.array(pb.p); X2 = np.array(pb.X)
    ax.plot_surface(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.4, label=label))

ax.plot(X_crit * 100, T_crit - 273.15, p_crit / 1e5, color='red', lw=2)
legend.append(Line2D([], [], color='red', lw=2, label='Critical curve'))
ax.plot(Xv_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='red',   lw=1)
ax.plot(Xl_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='green', lw=1)

ax.set_xlabel('Salinity (wt% NaCl)', fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel('Temperature (°C)',    fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_zlabel('Pressure (bar)',      fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 1000); ax.set_zlim(0, 2500)
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-145)
ax.set_title(r'H$_2$O–NaCl phase boundaries in T–p–X space', fontsize=13, pad=12)
ax.legend(handles=legend, loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.88)   # leaves room for the axis labels
plt.show()

docs.title: VLH coexistence surface
docs.text:
The three-phase vapour + liquid + halite (VLH) surface is parameterised by temperature. The left panel shows the coexistence pressure; the right panel shows the saturated liquid (halite liquidus) and vapour compositions along the surface.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

T = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, H2ONaCl.T_MAX_VLH, 200)   # K
P_vlh = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T))                                  # Pa
XL_vlh, XV_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T, P_vlh))                 # kg/kg

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))

axes[0].plot(T - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Pressure (bar)")
axes[0].set_title("VLH coexistence pressure")

axes[1].plot(T - 273.15, XL_vlh * 100, label="Liquid (halite liquidus)")
axes[1].plot(T - 273.15, XV_vlh * 100, label="Vapour")
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Salinity (wt% NaCl)")
axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

docs.title: Critical curve
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

T = np.linspace(sw.Tmin(), sw.Tmax(), 200)     # K
P_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T))  # Pa, kg/kg

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(T - 273.15, P_crit / 1e5)
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("Critical pressure (bar)")
ax.set_title("H\u2082O\u2013NaCl critical curve")
